The Vandals were a Germanic people who established a powerful naval kingdom in North Africa under Gaiseric, becoming among the most feared of the Germanic successor states. They sacked Rome itself in 455, and Gaiseric led this assault with devastating thoroughness, systematically plundering the city and targeting the wealth of the Roman elite—an even more complete devastation than Alaric's sack forty-five years earlier. The Vandals conquered North Africa, including the rich province of Africa Proconsularis, cutting off grain supplies to Rome and destabilizing the Western Empire's economy. They controlled a powerful fleet that dominated the Mediterranean, raiding coasts across the Roman world and extracting tribute from major powers. Gaiseric established a centralized kingdom based in Carthage, consolidating Vandal rule and passing the throne to his heirs in a stable succession. Yet the Vandals' reputation darkened due to their extreme religious intolerance toward Catholics. They favored Arian Christianity and persecuted Catholic populations, a legacy that shaped how later Christian chroniclers portrayed them. This harsh religious policy ultimately damaged their standing in posterity. The Vandal kingdom fell to Justinian I's reconquest, which lasted from 533 to 534 under the general Belisarius. The Vandal kingdom collapsed rapidly and was absorbed into the Byzantine Empire. The term "vandalism," meaning senseless destruction, derives from stereotypes of their destructiveness, though modern historians recognize that the kingdom was far more sophisticated than that term suggests.
